object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account in the subscription system, identified by a unique six-digit sequential account number that is never reused.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A unique six-digit sequential identifier for an Account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a specified cycle for a specified product, identified by a unique subscription ID prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionID
object_types.definition: A unique generated identifier for a Subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product that can be subscribed to. There are currently three products: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artefact that specifies what a customer pays and how often, identified by a plan code such as CORE-MO-49 or CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing what the customer receives, identified by its name. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Specifies how many seats, whether API and SSO are included.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The name of a FeatureBundle, serving as its unique identifier.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, identified by a change ID, with an effective date that may differ from the date the change was requested.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.

It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: ChangeID
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a Subscription begins. Mandatory field.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: SubscriptionEndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a Subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency at which a Subscription is billed: either Monthly or Annual. Exactly one per subscription, never neither, never both.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a Subscription. Exactly one of: Trialing, Active, PastDue, Cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.
Exactly one, yes.

object_types.definition: The date on which a PlanChange takes effect.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or entity that requested a PlanChange.

ambiguities.description: Plan terminology is overloaded. Stakeholders use 'plan' to refer to three distinct concepts: (1) PricePlan (the billing artefact with code like CORE-MO-49), (2) FeatureBundle (the feature set like Professional/Starter shown on pricing page), and (3) bespoke sales deals negotiated per customer (not modeled). The document will use separate names (PricePlan and FeatureBundle) but this ambiguity exists in the business and will cause communication issues. No clarification needed for the model, but stakeholders should be aware.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan?... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... And I mean the billing artefact... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Paused subscriptions: The system has a separate boolean 'paused' flag that overlaps with the four defined statuses (Trialing, Active, PastDue, Cancelled). A paused subscription can be active according to the status field but paused according to the flag, causing bugs. It is unclear whether 'paused' should be a fifth status or whether it is a temporary operational state orthogonal to status. The model captures the four formal statuses as specified, but the paused flag's relationship to status is undecided.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... It behaves like a status... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term annual subscription cancellation policy: When an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term, the system sets an end date to the paid-through date and access continues (no refund). However, the business rule is unclear. Sales implies refunds are possible, finance has given four refunds as goodwill in the last quarter, and the formal policy is undecided (requires finance and legal approval). The model captures the current system behaviour (end date set, access runs to it), but whether this is the intended business rule remains unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans. Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens?... The model will capture the system behaviour, which is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is derived from the PricePlan price and BillingPeriod (e.g., annual 490 = MRR 40.83). It appears in reporting dashboards but is not stored as an attribute in the source system. The model treats it as a derived calculation, not a stored fact, to avoid drift. However, it is unclear whether MRR should be cached/materialized for performance in the reporting layer, or whether it should be computed on-demand.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: Current plan denormalization: The subscription record carries a 'current plan' field that is denormalised and maintained by the plan change process. If the change history and current plan ever disagree, the change history is considered authoritative and the current plan is treated as a bug. It is unclear whether the current plan should be modeled as a derived fact (computed from change history) or as a stored attribute (as it actually exists in the data). The model treats it as a stored fact-type relationship but flags this as a potential consistency risk.

source_references.excerpt: it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Product set is fixed today: Three products exist (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) with a fourth in discovery. The value constraint on ProductCode reflects the current known set, but future products are expected. It is unclear whether the model should hardcode the constraint to these three, or use it as an illustration with the understanding that new products will be added.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Feature bundle as entity: FeatureBundle is treated as an entity type identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) and referenced by PricePlan. However, bundles have complex internal structure (seat counts, API access, SSO capability) that is not modeled in detail. It is unclear whether FeatureBundle should be decomposed into separate value types (e.g., BundleMaxSeats, BundleHasAPI, BundleHasSSO), or whether it should remain a black box entity. The model captures the bundle name as the identifier but does not reflect the internal structure.

source_references.excerpt: It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
